researcher: Codex parallel africa-regional-states-first research, integrated by Codex

sources.title: Robert Launay: Beyond the Stream, 1992
sources.note: Chapter 3, printed pages 50 to 51: Seku Wattara, regional power, commercial continuity and limits of direct control. Modern Korhogo ethnography is not silently attributed to old Kong.

sources.title: Mahir Şaul: The War Houses of the Watara in West Africa
sources.note: 1998 original research summarized in scholarly bibliography: household organization, dependants, warfare and trade. Used only for the summarized findings.

sources.title: Louis-Gustave Binger: Du Niger au golfe de Guinée, volume 1, 1892
sources.note: Chapter X, account of February and March 1888. Printed pages 297, 321, 326 and 331 to 332. Colonial officer’s observations explicitly attributed; his racial judgments, literacy generalizations and faulty foundation chronology are not adopted.

sources.title: ICOMOS: Evaluation of northern Ivorian mosques, 2021
sources.note: Printed pages 317 to 318: earthen masonry, protruding maintenance timbers, climate adaptations and small Kong mosque dating. Contains an unrelated erroneous seventeenth-century dating of the Moroccan invasion, not used here.

sources.title: UNESCO: Decision 44 COM 8B.33
sources.note: 2021 inscription; integrity and management sections identify 1897 destruction of the great Kong mosque, community reconstruction and living conservation.

sources.title: Coleman Donaldson: Jula Ajami in Burkina Faso, 2013
sources.note: Original research based on 2012 fieldwork. Indexed primary PDF read; direct fetch returned 403. Printed pages 30 to 31 distinguish Kong Jula register and explicitly state none of the participants was born or raised in Kong. Modern Latin transcription, not reconstructed Arabic-script text. Kong’s historical Arabic sample instead comes from Binger’s reproduced safe-conduct.

sources.title: Roland Oliver and Anthony Atmore: Africa since 1800, fifth edition
sources.note: Publisher preview; indexed opening chapter read. Post-1591 retreat and independent government in Dendi. Direct fetch timed out.

sources.title: Anne Haour and colleagues: The settlement mound of Birnin Lafiya, 2016
sources.note: Author manuscript read directly, printed pages 2 to 8. Fourth to thirteenth-century regional archaeology, explicitly not evidence of the later kingdom’s household customs.

sources.title: Paulo Fernando de Moraes Farias: Bentyia (Kukyia), 2013
sources.note: Original historical and epigraphic study; indexed full text paragraphs 104 to 108 checked. Distinguishes river Dendi from older Borgu trading communities.

sources.title: Republic of Niger: Counter-memorial in the Benin boundary case, 2004
sources.note: Primary party pleading, not a neutral court finding. Paragraphs 1.12 and 1.16 reproduce separate 1895 Gaya and 1897 Karimama treaty evidence; historical claims about unified sovereignty are disputed. Used for attributed documentary evidence and colonial transition, not endorsement of territorial arguments.

sources.title: Olivier Gosselain and Laurence Smolderen: Mission dans le Dendi et le Borgou, 2013
sources.note: Indexed original field report, printed page 82: Kompanti interviews on 31 January 2013, foundation traditions and named occupations. Direct repository redirect failed; indexed witness checked.

sources.title: Alexandre Livingstone Smith and Nicolas Nikis: Kompanti, 2018
sources.note: Indexed author chapter, printed pages 336 to 338, in Two Thousand Years in Dendi. Fieldwork on 26 January 2014; interpretation explicitly tentative.

sources.title: Olufunke Adeboye: The Church Graveyard, Ibadan 1853 to 1960
sources.note: Original archival research manuscript, pages 1, 5 and 9; nineteenth-century political character, home burial and named carpenters. Avoids generalizing every Yoruba mortuary practice to every household.

sources.title: Friedrich Wilhelm Schwerdtfeger: Comparative Study of Conventional Urban Houses, 1975
sources.note: Indexed thesis chapter 8 and chapter 11, printed page 174 read. Repository metadata https://soas-repository.worktribe.com/output/389511 confirms 1967 to 1969 fieldwork and author. Traditional courtyard model is a retrospective description, not all surveyed houses.

sources.title: Samuel Johnson: The History of the Yorubas, chapter XXV
sources.note: Original history completed in the nineteenth century, edited by Obadiah Johnson and first published in 1921. Publisher chapter extract on wartime farm defense checked.

sources.title: Samuel Johnson: The History of the Yorubas, chapter XXXII
sources.note: Publisher extract, printed pages 584 to 605: unfinished diplomacy following the 1886 Kiriji settlement.

sources.title: Dictionary of African Christian Biography: Anna Hinderer
sources.note: Scholarly biography drawing on missionary correspondence; Entering the Lion’s Den, Swimming against the Current and Mother, Playfellow, and Teacher. Specific observations attributed; missionary cultural and religious judgments are not adopted.

sources.title: Toyin Falola: Kemi Morgan and the Second Reconstruction of Ibadan History
sources.note: Original historiographical research, publisher extract: Akinyele’s 1911 Yoruba history and May public lecture. Short title reproduced as cited, without supplying unverified diacritics.

sources.title: Toyin Falola: Early Yoruba Historiography
sources.note: Indexed bibliographic note explicitly identifies The Outlines of Ibadan History as the English version of Iwe Itan Ibadan. Supports short title translation.

sources.title: University of Ibadan: About Us
sources.note: Institution’s own history, founding in 1948, initial military hospital site, 104 foundation students and lease of permanent site.

sources.title: Metropolitan Museum of Art: Nyanyeru and the history of Takrur
sources.note: Curatorial historical context identifies eleventh-century Senegal valley state and thirteenth-century Mali ascendancy. The nineteenth-century instrument is not claimed as a medieval Takrur artifact.

sources.title: Hatice Uğur: Tekrûr, TDV İslâm Ansiklopedisi, 2011
sources.note: Academic encyclopedia; Arabic headword, War Jabi, al-Idrisi’s trade account and al-Qazwini’s mixed community. Avoided overbroad first-Muslim and universal-conversion assertions.

sources.title: Umar al-Naqar: Takrur, The History of a Name, 1969
sources.note: Community-hosted complete reproduction of original Journal of African History article, volume 10, pages 365 to 374. Medieval sources and later broad usage; quoted historical translations treated as attributed accounts.

sources.title: Susan Keech McIntosh and Hamady Bocoum: New Perspectives on Sincu Bara, 2000
sources.note: Original excavation article read in full indexed text. Regional site evidence, not asserted identification of Takrur’s capital. Revised copper chronology and decorated objects.

sources.title: Daphne Gallagher, Susan McIntosh and Shawn Murray: Agriculture and wild plant use in the Middle Senegal River Valley, 2015
sources.note: Proceedings chapter printed pages 105 to 107, PDF pages 103 to 105: seven sites, charred seed/fruit analysis, pearl millet and variable wild plants; no confirmed rice or cotton in examined assemblages.

sources.title: David Killick: Changes in iron-smelting technology in the Senegal River valley
sources.note: Original research abstract for the 13th PanAfrican Archaeological Congress, Dakar: numerous furnace sites and sixteen radiocarbon dates. No assumption that all counted furnaces operated simultaneously or belonged to one kingdom.

batchIdentityNotes.assessment: Verified missing. Imported 1783 to 1914 polygon spans 7.48 to 12.33 N and 5.55 to 3.34 W. A narrative about the capital and connected regional houses is appropriate; broad outline is not asserted as uniform territorial administration. Historical rise predates import; 1897 destruction distinguished from map endpoint.

Post-1591 independent successor government established by Cambridge history; later regional unity is contested in primary ICJ pleadings. Avoided unsupported exact 1901 last-king claim; no alias proposed.
